📦 How to Install and Use the {bfo.db} Package in R

This guide will walk you through installing and using the bfo.db R package to interact with the BFO database.

✅ Step 1: Check Your R Version

Make sure you are using R version 4.1.0 or newer.

You can check your version in RStudio:

  • Look at the Console tab (top-left by default)
  • Or run one of the following commands:
Check version via terminal:

Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell):

R --version

macOS / Ubuntu / Linux (Terminal):

R --version

📦 Step 2: Install the pak Package (If Not Installed)

pak is a modern R package manager. Install it by running:

install.packages("pak")

🔄 You might be prompted to confirm installation of dependencies—click “Yes” or type y in the console.

Wait until you see a message like:

✔ DONE (pak)

🔌 Step 3: Install the {bfo.db} Package

To install the bfo.db package (recommended version v0.3.0), run:

pak::pak("Barefoot-Ocean/bfo.db@v0.3.0", upgrade = TRUE)

This version is recommended for stable database interaction.

📚 Step 4: Load the Package

Once installed, load the package:

library(bfo.db)

🔐 Step 5: Set Up Your Database Credentials

To connect, the package needs five pieces of information about the database:

Field What it is Example
dbname The database name bfo
host The server address bfo.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
port The network port 5432
user Your database username jane.doe
password Your database password ••••••••

(Ask the Barefoot Ocean data team for these values if you don’t have them.)

It also needs an SSL certificate — but you don’t have to worry about that: the package ships one and uses it automatically (see 5d. Choosing the SSL certificate, below).

🛡️ The one rule that matters: your user and password are secrets. Never paste them into a file that is shared, emailed, or committed to GitHub. Every recommended method below keeps your secrets in a file that stays only on your computer.

Which method should I use?

There are three ways to provide your credentials. If you’re not sure, use Method A.

Method Best for Your secrets live in
A. A config.yml file Most people; a single analyst on one computer a local config.yml (kept off GitHub)
B. config.yml + .Renviron Teams and shared projects with many users each person’s own .Renviron
C. Typed into the script Quick one-off tests only the script itself ⚠️

Method A — Use a config.yml file (recommended for most people)

A config.yml is a small text file that holds your connection settings. You create it once and reuse it.

1. Create the file. In RStudio, run this to create and open it in the project you’re working in:

file.edit("config.yml")

2. Paste in this template and replace each XXXXXX with your real values (keep the indentation — YAML cares about spaces, and use 2 spaces, not tabs):

default:
  bfo_data:
    dbname: XXXXXX
    host: XXXXXX
    port: XXXXXX
    user: XXXXXX
    password: XXXXXX
  # Optional — omit this line to use the certificate bundled with the package.
  # ssl_key: path/to/your-own-cert.pem

Save the file (Ctrl/Cmd + S).

3. Connect, pointing at the file you just created:

db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "config.yml")

4. Keep it private. If your project is a Git repository, make sure config.yml is never committed:

usethis::use_git_ignore("config.yml")   # adds it to .gitignore for you

If you’re not using usethis, just add a line containing config.yml to your .gitignore file by hand.

Method B — config.yml + .Renviron (recommended for teams / many users)

When several people share the same project (e.g. on GitHub), you don’t want everyone’s passwords sitting in a shared config.yml. The clean pattern is:

  • a single, shareable config.yml that contains no secrets — it only refers to environment variables; and
  • a personal .Renviron file on each person’s computer that holds their own secret values.

This way the same project works for many users, and each person’s password never leaves their own machine.

1. Open your personal .Renviron. The easiest way is with usethis:

# install.packages("usethis")   # if you don't have it yet
usethis::edit_r_environ()            # opens your personal (user-level) .Renviron
# usethis::edit_r_environ("project") # or one just for the current project

This opens (creating it if needed) a file where you store secrets as NAME=value, one per line. .Renviron is not R code — no quotes, no spaces around =:

BFO_DB_NAME=bfo
BFO_DB_HOST=bfo.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
BFO_DB_PORT=5432
BFO_DB_USER=jane.doe
BFO_DB_PASSWORD=your-secret-password

💡 Where does this file live? Your user-level .Renviron is in your home folder (~/.Renviron). You normally never need to find it by hand — usethis::edit_r_environ() opens it for you.

2. Save the file and restart R. .Renviron is only read when R starts, so restart your session (in RStudio: Session → Restart R) for the new values to take effect.

3. Write a config.yml that reads those variables instead of holding the secrets directly. The !expr tag tells R to run a small expression — Sys.getenv("…") simply looks up a value from .Renviron:

default:
  bfo_data:
    dbname: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_NAME")
    host: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_HOST")
    port: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_PORT")
    user: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_USER")
    password: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_PASSWORD")

Because this file contains no real secrets, it is safe to commit and share.

4. Connect exactly as in Method A:

db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "config.yml")
Advanced: several connection profiles in one file

config.yml can hold more than one named profile (for example a read-only and an admin login, or a staging server). Add extra top-level blocks and switch between them with the R_CONFIG_ACTIVE environment variable:

default:
  bfo_data:
    dbname: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_NAME")
    host: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_HOST")
    port: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_PORT")
    user: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_READONLY_USER")
    password: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_READONLY_PASSWORD")

admin:
  bfo_data:
    dbname: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_NAME")
    host: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_HOST")
    port: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_PORT")
    user: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_ADMIN_USER")
    password: !expr Sys.getenv("BFO_ADMIN_PASSWORD")
Sys.setenv(R_CONFIG_ACTIVE = "admin")   # use the "admin" block; default is "default"
db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "config.yml")

Method C — Type credentials directly in your script (quick tests only)

You can pass everything straight to the connector. This is the fastest way to try a connection, but the password ends up in your script, so only use it for throwaway tests — and never save or share a script that contains a real password.

db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(
  dbname   = "bfo",
  host     = "bfo.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com",
  port     = 5432,
  user     = "jane.doe",
  password = "your-secret-password",
  sslmode  = "require"
  # sslrootcert is optional — see 5d below.
)

A safer middle ground is to keep the secrets in .Renviron (as in Method B) and read them in your script, so no password is ever written down:

db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(
  dbname   = Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_NAME"),
  host     = Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_HOST"),
  port     = Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_PORT"),
  user     = Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_USER"),
  password = Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_PASSWORD")
)

5d. 🔏 Choosing the SSL certificate (the .pem file)

The connection is encrypted (sslmode = "require"), which needs the AWS RDS Certificate Authority (CA) bundle to verify the server’s identity. Good news:

  • This is not a secret. It’s a public certificate published by AWS, so it’s completely safe to share or commit.
  • You don’t have to manage it. The package ships the AWS CA bundles inside itself, and uses them automatically.

Most users should do nothing here — just omit sslrootcert (and ssl_key), and the package uses the global bundle (which works for every AWS region), falling back to the us-east-1 bundle. The defaults resolve to:

system.file("cert", "global-bundle.pem", package = "bfo.db")   # used by default
system.file("cert", "us-east-1-bundle.pem", package = "bfo.db") # fallback

You only need to choose a certificate yourself in special cases:

You want to… In config.yml set… In a direct call set…
Use the default (recommended) (leave ssl_key out) (leave sslrootcert out)
Force the region bundle ssl_key: !expr system.file("cert", "us-east-1-bundle.pem", package = "bfo.db") sslrootcert = system.file("cert", "us-east-1-bundle.pem", package = "bfo.db")
Use your own certificate ssl_key: /path/to/your-cert.pem sslrootcert = "/path/to/your-cert.pem"

If you ever need the newest bundle straight from AWS, download it from:

  • Global: https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem
  • Region: https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/us-east-1/us-east-1-bundle.pem

📅 Step 6: Fetch Data from the Database

You can fetch data in two ways depending on your workflow:

Option A: Load All Data Immediately 

global_ref_data <- db$collect_view("global_ref")

Option B: Work with the Database Object First (More Memory-Efficient) 

global_ref_data <- db$get_view("global_ref")
# You can apply filters, joins, etc. before collecting:
global_ref_data <- global_ref_data |>
      dplyr::filter(country == "IDN") |>
      dplyr::collect()

🔒 Step 7: Close the Database Connection

Once you’re done, return the pooled connections and close the pool:

db$close()        # (db$disconnect() is an alias)

close() is safe to call more than once, and if you forget, the pool is also closed automatically when the object is garbage-collected.

✅ Putting it all together

A complete session, from connecting to closing (using a config.yml as in Method A):

library(bfo.db)

# 1. Connect
db <- DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "config.yml")

# 2. Pull a table into R
countries <- db$collect_view("global_ref")

# 3. ...or query lazily and let the database do the work first
idn_sites <- db$get_view("global_ref") |>
  dplyr::filter(country == "IDN") |>
  dplyr::collect()

# 4. Always close when you're done
db$close()

💡 Don’t want the step-by-step messages? Add quiet = TRUE when you connect: DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "config.yml", quiet = TRUE).

⚠️ Notes: Possible Issues and Solutions

Connection problems

Message you see What it usually means How to fix it
All connection parameters are required… A field (often password) is empty or misspelled Check your config.yml/.Renviron; remember .Renviron needs an R restart
could not connect to server / timeout Wrong host/port, or you’re not on the right network/VPN Confirm the values with the data team and your network access
password authentication failed Wrong user or password Re-check those two values
Values from .Renviron come back empty R was not restarted after editing .Renviron Session → Restart R, then try again
Cannot open lock file: Permission denied during install R is installing into a folder you don’t own Install into a personal library; see the install notes

A quick way to check your .Renviron values loaded correctly (this prints the host, not your password):

Sys.getenv("BFO_DB_HOST")

GitHub access (for installing the package)

  1. GitHub Access: Make sure you are a member of the Barefoot-Ocean organization on GitHub. If not, you won’t be able to access the private repository.

  2. Authentication Token (Optional but Recommended): Adding a GitHub token to your .Renviron file helps avoid GitHub rate limits during package installation.

Add a GitHub Token to .Renviron

Step-by-step instructions:

💻 On Windows:

  1. Open RStudio.

  2. Run usethis::edit_r_environ() to open your .Renviron file.

  3. Add the following line (replace your_token):

    GITHUB_PAT=your_token

  4. Save and close the file.

  5. Restart RStudio.

💻 On macOS/Linux:

  1. Open Terminal.

  2. Edit the .Renviron file in your home directory (or use RStudio as above):

    open -a TextEdit ~/.Renviron  # for macOS
nano ~/.Renviron              # for CLI edit

  3. Add the line:

    GITHUB_PAT=your_token

  4. Save the file and restart RStudio.

You can create a new token at: https://github.com/settings/tokens

Development notes (only for developers)

bfo.db is an R package that facilitates database connections and view retrieval using RPostgres, pool, and other related packages.

Installation

You can install the development version of bfo.db from GitHub:

devtools::install_github("Barefoot-Ocean/bfo.db")
remotes::install_github("Barefoot-Ocean/bfo.db")

Usage

This is a basic example:

# Load the package
library(bfo.db)

# Example of initializing a database connection with a configuration file
db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "path/to/config.yml")

# Example of initializing a database connection with credentials
# (sslrootcert is optional; defaults to the bundled AWS RDS us-east-1 CA bundle)
db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(dbname = XXXXXXX,
                                    host = XXXXXXX,
                                    user = XXXXXXX,
                                    password = "XXXXXXX",
                                    port = XXXXXXX,
                                    sslmode = "require"
                                    )

# Retrieve a view from the database
view_connection <- db$get_view("view_name")

# Close the database connection
db$close()

Get user information by email 

library(bfo.db)
db <- bfo.db::DatabaseConnector$new(config_path = "path/to/config.yml")

# Get user information by email
db$get_user_information(user_email = 'anastasiia@barefootocean.org')

Features

  • Easy initialization of database connections from a configuration file or direct parameters.
  • Retrieval of database views using get_view() method.
  • Informative, step-by-step console messages (set quiet = TRUE to silence).
  • Safe, idempotent pool cleanup via close()/disconnect(), with automatic cleanup on garbage collection.

Dependencies

  • R (>= 4.1.0; developed and tested on R 4.4)
  • DBI (== 1.2.3)
  • RPostgres (== 1.4.7)
  • dplyr (== 1.1.4)
  • dbplyr (== 2.5.0)
  • config (== 0.3.2)
  • stringr (== 1.5.1)
  • tibble (== 3.2.1)
  • pool (== 1.0.3)
  • R6 (== 2.6.1)
  • later (== 1.3.2)
  • rlang (== 1.1.6)
  • assertthat (== 0.2.1)
  • glue (== 1.7.0)
  • jsonlite (== 2.0.0)

Release process (maintainers)

The package uses renv for reproducible dependencies and ships the AWS RDS CA bundles under inst/cert/. To cut a new release:

  1. Make your code/doc changes.

  2. Bump Version: in DESCRIPTION and add an entry to NEWS.md.

  3. Regenerate docs and the README:

    roxygen2::roxygenise()        # updates NAMESPACE + man/
rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd")  # regenerates README.md

  4. Refresh the lockfile against your current R/library:

    renv::snapshot(type = "implicit", prompt = FALSE)

  5. Sanity-check the build (the CA bundles must appear under inst/cert/):

    devtools::build()

  6. Commit, tag, and push the release (tag must match the version so pak::pak("Barefoot-Ocean/bfo.db@vX.Y.Z") resolves):

    git tag v0.3.0
git push origin main --tags

  7. Optionally create a GitHub release from the tag.

To refresh the bundled certificates from AWS:

curl -fsSL -o inst/cert/global-bundle.pem \
  https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem
curl -fsSL -o inst/cert/us-east-1-bundle.pem \
  https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/us-east-1/us-east-1-bundle.pem
